summary: A modular monolith build: React SPA on the frontend, Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot for the backend, PostgreSQL for data, hosted on AWS ECS on Fargate for about $1,962-6,967 a month. It stays on AWS and keeps data in India under RBI localisation and PCI DSS, builds on the team's Java, and ships as one deployable that a team of 8 can build in 16 weeks.

frontend.choice: React SPA (Vite) + Native iOS + Android (Swift / Kotlin) for the Android/iOS app
frontend.justification: React SPA (Vite) is the frontend for a Fintech / payments / ledger project with about 60,000 daily users (~833 requests/s at peak), built by a team of 8 in 16 weeks. Search visibility is marked not needed (behind login), so rendering in the browser is acceptable, and it scores 5.0/5 for rich, app-like interaction. Angular is within 0.8 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); the tie went to React SPA (Vite) on lower vendor lock-in (6 vs 7, summed lock-in). You also target iOS/Android. Native iOS + Android (Swift / Kotlin) scored best among mobile toolkits with the same weights and backend. team.languages does not list Swift, so the iOS app (Swift) is a language the team must learn; React Native (Expo) would reuse the team's TypeScript instead.

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.8 points higher; the tie went to React SPA (Vite) on lower vendor lock-in (6 vs 7, summed lock-in); either is defensible. React SPA (Vite) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0), development speed (4.0 vs 3.0); Angular is stronger on structure for large teams (5.0 vs 2.0), team skill match (4.0 vs 3.5).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 1.2 points. React SPA (Vite) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0), portability (low lock-in) (5.0 vs 4.0); Next.js (React) is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), development speed (5.0 vs 4.0); Next.js (React) takes a penalty: No search visibility needed: server rendering adds a Node.js server for pages that React SPA (Vite) serves as static files.
Ruled out: Mobile toolkit; web is a target, so the primary frontend is a web framework (mobile app suggested as companion)

tradeoffs: Client-side rendering: the first screen waits for the JavaScript bundle to download and run
Routing, data fetching and state are your own architecture decisions

The team lists Java and Kotlin, so it needs no new server language (team skill match 5.0/5). It runs as a long-running Java/Kotlin service, so background jobs and database connection pools live in one deployable process. It leads the runner-up, Go (net/http, chi or Gin), by 3.0 stack points (points of the overall stack score, the average of the four layer scores).

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.0 points. Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot is stronger on team skill match (5.0 vs 3.5), ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 4.0); Go (net/http, chi or Gin) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 3.0), performance / latency (5.0 vs 4.0).

database.justification: Your data is mainly relational and reaches about 411 GB within 12 months; PostgreSQL fits relational data 5/5. Strong consistency is assumed, since no input says stale reads are acceptable, and PostgreSQL gives it: a read after a write always sees that write. Its share of the estimated bill is $800-$2,502 a month, against a total budget of $6,000 a month. MySQL is within 0.1 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); PostgreSQL has the higher stack score.

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.1 points lower; either is defensible. PostgreSQL is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 6.8 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on data-model fit (5.0 vs 2.0), consistency fit (5.0 vs 3.5); MongoDB is stronger on team skill match (3.5 vs 1.5), scalability (5.0 vs 4.0); MongoDB takes a penalty: Only 2/5 fit for your primary 'relational' data.
Ruled out: Eventually consistent; cannot be the system of record for ACID data; In-memory store: ~411 GB within 12 months cannot sensibly live in RAM as the system of record (use it as a cache)
Ruled out: Eventually consistent; cannot be the system of record for ACID data

tradeoffs: Single-writer primary: write scale-out needs sharding (Citus) or Aurora Limitless
Connection-per-process model needs PgBouncer/RDS Proxy under serverless

hosting.choice: AWS ECS on Fargate, region ap-south-1 (Mumbai)
hosting.justification: AWS ECS on Fargate hosts the stack for users in India at a 99.95% availability target. It runs the Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot API as long-running processes, sized for ~833 requests/s at peak. For PCI DSS it is a validated service provider, so card-handling infrastructure can sit on it. Its share of the estimated bill is $800-$2,904 a month, against a total budget of $6,000 a month. It leads the runner-up, AWS Lambda + API Gateway, by 2.9 stack points.

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 2.9 points. AWS ECS on Fargate is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), portability (low lock-in) (3.0 vs 2.0); AWS Lambda + API Gateway is stronger on team skill match (3.5 vs 1.5), low ops burden (5.0 vs 3.0). A stack compatibility rule costs it 4.5 points, more than the whole gap, while on this layer's own criteria it is 1.6 points ahead: Large frameworks suffer cold starts on Lambda (SnapStart helps Java); containers on ECS/Cloud Run fit better.
Ruled out for your answers: Not on AWS, the cloud you require.

supporting.choice: Amazon SQS with Spring Cloud AWS listeners
supporting.justification: Send emails, process uploads and call slow APIs outside the request path. Sized for the 300,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.choice: Doing the work inside the web request
alternatives.why_not: Slow emails, uploads and API calls would hold the request open and fail with it

tradeoffs: A job can run twice after a retry, so handlers must be idempotent

supporting.choice: Amazon S3, a private bucket in your required region (short-lived signed URLs, no public CDN)
supporting.justification: Uploaded files and video belong in object storage, not the database. Hand uploads out from the bucket, not the app server; a public CDN would cache copies at edge sites outside the country your data must stay in, and each signed URL expires within minutes. The scenario stores 500 GB within 12 months (scale.data_volume_gb_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: They bloat backups and the database disk, which costs several times more per GB than object storage

alternatives.choice: Serving files through the app server
alternatives.why_not: Each download holds an app connection and pays the app host's egress price

tradeoffs: Files and their database rows can drift apart: delete or replace both together
Links that leak can be shared until they expire, so keep their lifetime short

supporting.justification: One-time codes need an SMS gateway with rate limits against SMS-pumping fraud; Indian operators deliver only DLT-registered templates. MSG91 stores its data only in India (Google Cloud, Mumbai) according to its 2024 data-localisation audit, which notes some processing in Singapore with the data brought back to India; Twilio Verify runs in Twilio's US region (twilio.com/docs/global-infrastructure), so codes and phone numbers would be processed and stored outside India. The SMS gateway runs outside AWS, which your cloud rule requires for the servers and data: only phone numbers and codes pass through it. Sized for the 300,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: Twilio runs Verify in its US region, so codes and numbers would be processed and stored outside India
Every user must install an app first, which loses sign-ups on a consumer product

tradeoffs: Each SMS is paid, and open sign-up forms invite SMS-pumping fraud: rate-limit by number and IP

supporting.choice: Spring Security's one-time token login in your API, with one-time codes sent through the SMS gateway and the users in your database in your Indian region: Amazon Cognito would cost about $4,350 a month at ~300,000 monthly users
supporting.justification: Do not hand-roll password storage, MFA or SSO. Sized for the 300,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

warnings.message: Budget below the top of the estimate. $1,962-$6,967/month against $6,000/month: the top (~3x today's load) is over, most of the rise in AWS ECS on Fargate and PostgreSQL. Raise the budget before the load grows.

Native app in a language the team did not list. team.languages does not list Swift, so the iOS app (Swift) is a language the team must learn; React Native (Expo) would reuse the team's TypeScript instead. Plan time to learn it or hire for it before the first release.

Card payments: the hosted checkout collects card numbers on the payment provider's page, so your PCI DSS check is the shortest self-assessment (SAQ A). Putting card fields on your own pages, or storing card numbers, widens the audit.
DPDP Act 2023: collect personal data with a clear notice and consent, let users see, correct and erase it, and report a breach to the Data Protection Board and the people affected.

RBI localisation: the entire payment data must be stored only in India, so backups, replicas and logs that hold it must also be in an Indian region; check each destination before go-live (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/NotificationUser.aspx?Id=11244).

assumptions: project.description sets no field in a scenario file: every choice comes from the structured fields, so wording cannot move the stack (in the app, the description reader only suggests fields for you to confirm); a fixed keyword list adds the 'Read from project.description' notes, which change no pick

Read from project.description ('UPI'): use a payment gateway that takes UPI collections, UPI AutoPay mandates for repeat debits such as EMIs, and payouts to users' accounts through its payout API (Razorpay and Cashfree offer all three)

Read from project.description ('KYC'): identity documents are sensitive personal data: keep them in the private object store with server-side encryption, open them only through short-lived signed URLs, log every access, and keep them as long as the regulator requires (RBI's KYC Master Direction: at least five years after the relationship ends)

Read from project.description ('double-entry'): write each money movement as balanced debit and credit rows in one database transaction, append-only (a correction is a new reversing entry, never an edit), and derive balances from the rows
Read from project.description ('credit scoring'): version the scoring model and store which version scored each application with its inputs, so every decision can be explained and replayed later
Sized for scale.users_12_months: 300,000 users, about 60,000 active on a day (20% daily-to-monthly ratio); scale.users_at_launch (10,000) is the starting point
rbi_localisation: RBI's 2018 directive on storage of payment system data requires payment data to be stored only in India, so every store must have an Indian region
iso27001: only hosts and managed services (backend-as-a-service, managed-only databases) that publish ISO/IEC 27001 certification are kept

compliance: DPDP Act 2023 (in force through the DPDP Rules 2025, notified November 2025 and phased in over 18 months) allows cross-border transfer except to notified countries, so it adds consent/breach-notice duties but not an India-region filter. Set infrastructure.data_residency to india if a sector rule (e.g. RBI) applies.

Stored data: The stated 500 GB counts uploaded files too. The database is sized for ~411 GB of rows (0.5 MB per daily user a month for this app type, at ~64,782 daily users, launch plus 12 months), and the other ~89 GB of files is priced as object storage on the stack's cloud.
